issues.legal_issue: Permission to transfer land assigned to a protected beneficiary must be refused when the proposed transfer conflicts with the constitutional or legal protections governing the assignment.
material_facts: The land belonged to the State and had been allotted to a tribal beneficiary.
The appellant agreed to purchase the land, subject to the Collector’s permission, and sought permission to alienate it.
The Collector and Commissioner refused permission, broadly on the ground that the assigned land could not be sold or converted to non-agricultural use.
The appellant challenged the refusal, and the High Court dismissed the challenge.
issues.conclusion: The refusal of permission was consistent with the constitutional scheme and was justified.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 14, 21, 38, 39 and 46 of the Constitution, read with the Preamble, the State must protect weaker sections from exploitation and promote their economic interests. Before granting permission to alienate assigned land, the competent authority must examine the nature of the property, pre-existing rights, and whether the proposed transaction violates the Constitution or the law; if it does, permission must be refused.

predicates.appeal_challenging_permission_refusal: A person appeals after an authority has refused permission for a proposed transfer of land.
predicates.land_assigned_to_protected_beneficiary: The land was assigned by the State to a beneficiary whose economic interests receive special protection.
predicates.proposed_transfer_conflicts_with_assignm: The proposed transfer is inconsistent with the legal or constitutional protections governing the assigned land.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges refusal of permission to transfer protected assigned land, and the proposed transfer conflicts with the protections governing the assignment, the refusal is justified.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to transfer protected assigned land in breach of the protections governing its alienation is void as opposed to public policy.
material_facts: The State had allotted the land to a tribal beneficiary.
The beneficiary entered into an agreement to sell the land, subject to the Collector’s permission.
The authorities refused permission, and the proposed sale was inconsistent with the protection against alienation of the assigned land.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was void under section 23 of the Contract Act as opposed to public policy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Contract Act renders an agreement void when its object or consideration is opposed to public policy. The Court relied on DTC v. DTC Mazdoor Congress and held that restrictions on alienation of assigned land give effect to the constitutional policy of economic empowerment and protection of weaker sections, including under Articles 14, 21, 38, 39 and 46.

predicates.agreement_to_transfer_protected_assigned: A beneficiary and another person made an agreement to transfer land assigned for the beneficiary’s protection.
predicates.transfer_lacks_required_permission: The transfer was subject to official permission and that permission was not obtained.
predicates.transfer_defeats_protective_policy: The proposed transfer would defeat the protections intended to preserve the assigned land for the beneficiary or protected group.

issues.definition: An agreement to transfer protected assigned land is void when the required permission was not obtained and the transfer would defeat the protections attached to the land.

issues.legal_issue: The protection for possession under part performance is unavailable where possession rests on an agreement for a transfer that was not authorized and is void.
material_facts: The appellant entered into possession pursuant to the agreement to purchase the assigned land.
The agreement was subject to permission for alienation, which the authorities refused.
The Court held that the agreement was void and that the appellant’s possession was unlawful.
issues.conclusion: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply, and the appellant’s possession remained unlawful.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act did not protect possession founded on the void, unauthorized agreement in this case; the Court held that the appellant’s possession was unlawful.

predicates.claim_based_on_part_performance: A possessor relies on part performance of an agreement as a basis for retaining the property.
predicates.possession_under_unapproved_transfer_agr: The possessor entered or remained in possession under an agreement for a transfer that required permission, but permission was not obtained.
predicates.transfer_agreement_is_void: The agreement for transfer is void because it conflicts with protections governing the property.

issues.definition: Part-performance protection is unavailable when the claimant possesses property under an unapproved transfer agreement that is void.

issues.legal_issue: A person in unlawful possession of assigned land is not entitled to compensation for improvements made to it.
material_facts: The appellant made improvements to the land after entering possession under the agreement.
The required permission for alienation had been refused, the agreement was void, and the Court held that the appellant’s possession was unlawful.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was not entitled to compensation for improvements made to the land.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the appellant’s unlawful possession as insufficient to give him a right to compensation for improvements made to the assigned land.

predicates.improvements_made_to_land: The possessor made improvements to land while occupying it.
predicates.possession_without_authorized_transfer: The possessor occupied the land without an authorized transfer.

issues.definition: A possessor who improves land while occupying it without an authorized transfer is not entitled to compensation for those improvements.

issues.legal_issue: Land assigned to a protected beneficiary that cannot lawfully be transferred must be resumed and assigned to an eligible protected beneficiary.
material_facts: The State had allotted the land to a tribal beneficiary.
The proposed transfer was not permitted, and the appellant’s possession was unlawful.
The Court directed the Collector to resume the land and assign it to the legal representatives of the original beneficiary if eligible, or otherwise to another eligible tribal beneficiary.
issues.conclusion: The Collector was directed to resume the land immediately and assign it to eligible legal representatives of the original beneficiary or to another eligible tribal beneficiary.
issues.legal_principle: The restrictions on alienation of assigned land implement the constitutional policy of economic empowerment under Articles 14, 21, 38, 39 and 46, read with the Preamble. Where the assignee is disqualified or unavailable, the land is to be resumed and assigned to an eligible successor or other eligible member of the protected group in accordance with that policy.

predicates.state_assigned_land_to_protected_benefic: The State assigned land to a beneficiary whose economic interests receive special protection.
predicates.attempted_transfer_is_not_permitted: A proposed transfer of the assigned land was not authorized.
predicates.current_possession_is_unlawful: The person currently possessing the land has no lawful basis for that possession.

issues.definition: When protected assigned land cannot lawfully be transferred and is unlawfully possessed, it must be resumed and assigned to an eligible protected beneficiary.
